term.def: A trick where hidden instructions are slipped into text, files or websites to make an AI tool act against the user's wishes. It is a growing risk as more teams connect AI to emails, documents and systems.

quiz.q: TechCrunch reports that Otter AI can now follow conversations across more than 30 languages.
quiz.why: This is exactly what the TechCrunch headline states about Otter AI's new language support.

quiz.q: Analytics India Magazine reports that Meta has launched pricing for its Muse AI agent in India.
quiz.why: This restates the headline about Meta Muse AI agent pricing launching in India.

quiz.q: An AI tool will always give the exact same answer to the exact same question.
quiz.why: Many AI tools add small random variation by design, so answers can differ slightly even for identical prompts.

quiz.q: AI tools can sound confident even when the answer they give is wrong.
quiz.why: AI models predict likely words, not verified truth, so confident wrong answers do happen and need human checking.

quiz.q: Once a company starts using AI tools, employees no longer need any training to use them well.
quiz.why: Good results still depend on clear prompts, context and judgement, which usually need some basic training.
